name: Opus 5 unrestricted
strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 25% because it is doing precisely what I bought it to do and I have no reason to touch it. It led all sectors in August on a 12-month basis at +16.0%, added over 1% in a week when the index made a record, and it does that at ~18x forward earnings with a 0.65-0.75 beta — the combination of leadership and low beta is rare and is exactly what makes a 48%-effective energy position carryable. The support is not just rotation: Q2 earnings beat broadly and the GLP-1 obesity franchise keeps compounding, so this is a sector with its own earnings engine rather than a defensive hiding place. Two cooling CPI prints and a Fed heading toward cuts is the regime where low-beta quality compounds. Still deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE: the whole point of making this the largest equity leg in a book that also runs a 2x energy fund is that it does not add variance. Still no stop, for the same reason as last week — this is the position I want to still own if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only ever fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I would want to be holding it.

Raised from 20% back above where I trimmed it, because the specific risk that drove the trim receded while the physical case got stronger. Last week I wrote that a written Iran-Oman proposal was a different order of risk than a rumour and that I would not run 52% effective XLE into it. That proposal has stalled: Iran conditions reopening on the US ending the war and meeting its terms, Trump claims total control of the strait, the Treasury Secretary has committed to an indefinite naval blockade plus unprecedented economic measures, attacks on shipping continued through 8/12, and — the detail that matters most — Hormuz vessel traffic FELL this week with tankers going dark, directly contradicting the official line that flows have normalised. Against that, the IEA doubled its Q3-2026 deficit estimate to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest quarterly deficit since Q4 2021, revising 3Q supply down 1.7 mb/d. A deficit that size draws inventories whether or not anyone signs anything. My convergence worry does not survive the longer frame either: XLE ran over 6% to $61.06 this week, but Brent traded above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and is $88.52 now — the market has faded the war premium into a worsening balance, which is the mispricing, and ERX at ~$99 against a 52-week high of $110.78 has not made the move the underlying has. This is 48% effective XLE and remains by far my largest directional risk. The honest bear case is unchanged and is one headline wide: a deal lands, crude gaps down, and a 2x fund halves the move twice over. That is why this is 24 and not 30, and it is why the true protection here is size rather than the stop, which would gap through on that headline. Stop tightened from -28% to -22%, capping the leg at ~5.3% of NAV — roughly an 11% XLE break, wide enough to survive the daily noise of a levered fund, tight enough to end the trade if the supply story genuinely breaks.

Held flat at 20% because it is still the only asset I own that wins in both tails of my own book, and nothing this week changed that. If the stalemate persists, gold keeps the geopolitical bid alongside ERX. If Iran and the US suddenly settle and crude collapses, taking ERX with it, that resolution lands on a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs against a +80k consensus with roughly 100k of prior downward revisions, and on a second consecutive cooling CPI at +0.1% m/m and 3.4% y/y — a Fed cutting into a softening economy is what gold is built for. Every other long leg here needs one of those two worlds; this one is indifferent to which arrives. The bid stays layered rather than single-source: rate-cut repricing, central-bank buying, a soft dollar, and the Hormuz premium. Still bullion rather than GDX — stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in exactly the thing I am trying to reduce. What I am respecting is that a 10% month above $4,400 and a Friday fade to ~$4,371 on profit-taking off a two-month high means this is extended near-term, so the stop comes in from -18% to -13%, capping the leg at 2.6% of NAV. That is still far outside any headline-driven shakeout but close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out of a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Raised from 6% to 10% — the first week since I put this on where both drivers cut the same way at the same time. The cost half, which was actively working against me last week when crude fell 5%, has flipped hard: Brent is back up over 5% to $88.52, jet fuel is spiking again, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% year over year, and the coverage has turned to how quickly fuel costs outpace revenue gains — carriers are rewriting earnings expectations, and record summer passenger volumes are now being described as masking a fragile margin story rather than as a bull case. The demand half is intact and independent of that: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically called out soft is a direct read on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure is the first cohort to flinch as fares climb to cover fuel. Crucially the tape finally confirmed — JETS fell 4% in a single session and extended a two-day decline after challenging all-time highs, so this is no longer a short fighting its own chart. The third reason is portfolio-level: with the S&P at a record close this is my only equity hedge and the only thing here that pays if the indices break. I accept that this doubles down on the same oil call as ERX and that a Hormuz deal costs me on both legs at once — that is the concentrated failure mode of this book and I am naming it rather than pretending it away. Squeeze risk stays specific and live: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a government equity stake, even with Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly preferring private funding. It is an ETF, so no single-name earnings gap. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is about 30bps a year. Stop -18% caps the leg at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25% for a smaller, faster exit.

Unchanged at 7%. Silver sits at $64.21 with the gold/silver ratio at 67.22, ticking down from 67.50 — the catch-up is grinding rather than accelerating, which is fine at this size. The thesis is the same dovish repricing that drives GLD, expressed with more beta: two cooling CPI prints and a Fed path toward cuts, on a metal up 67% over the past year. The ambivalence I flagged when I sized it is still the reason it is 7% and not 20%: silver carries an industrial demand component gold lacks, and a weakening labor market cuts against that component even as the monetary case strengthens. I keep respecting the instrument's own history — it traded to the mid-$80s in February and is $64 now, a drawdown that would have taken out any tight stop — so the stop stays wide in absolute terms. Tightened from -22% to -18% only because the leg has run with the metal; that caps it at 1.3% of NAV while still leaving room for ordinary silver noise, which is violent.

Held completely untouched for a second week, because literally nothing changed and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in fees and attention than it could earn. DOGE closed the week around $0.0699, flat over 24 hours, still pinned below $0.08 and still the weakest thing in its asset class. The edge remains structural rather than a market view: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage times 10% APR, so this 3x is genuinely free carry — I am being paid to hold a short on the worst horse in the race. The honest risk is unchanged: the same rate-cut repricing that makes my gold leg work lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies the tape in both directions, which is exactly why this stays 3% at 3x rather than anything larger. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin, the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV, and the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE down roughly 30% for about 1.8:1.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I cut energy from 26% to 20% last week for one stated reason: an Iran-Oman draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament made the de-escalation binary too live to run a 52% effective single-sector bet into. That reason weakened this week rather than strengthened. The accord is deadlocked, Iran has re-anchored on ending the war and sanctions relief as preconditions, the US has committed to an indefinite blockade, ship attacks continued, and Hormuz vessel traffic fell rather than normalised. At the same time the physical case got materially better: the IEA doubled its Q3 deficit to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest since Q4 2021, which draws barrels regardless of what any parliament does. And the reason I thought I had spent my cushion — XLE +6% on the week — does not survive the wider frame: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and sits at $88.52 today. The premium has been faded, not extended. So energy goes back up. The second change follows from the same fact: JETS is the only leg where both drivers turned my way in the same week, cost and demand, and it is simultaneously my only hedge against an S&P sitting at a record. I am funding both out of a 19% cash pile that was insurance against a resolution the week made less likely. The rest of the book is untouched in size — I am tightening stops on three legs that have run, because on a 2x fund and on metals up 10% in a month, size is the real protection and the stop only bounds what is left.
novelty: The overlap constraint does not bind me — I run no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction gross weight to test against; this is my only book and it remains a single concentrated oil-supply-shock expression carried by low-beta ballast.
research_notes:
Checked the five live drivers of this book against the 8/11-8/14 tape.

OIL / HORMUZ (the binary I sized down for last week): the de-escalation path has visibly receded. Iran and Oman have NOT reached agreement; Iran now says the strait "will remain closed unless the United States ends the war and meets Tehran's conditions," Trump counters that the US has "total control," and the Treasury Secretary committed to unprecedented economic measures plus an indefinite naval blockade of Iranian ports. Ship attacks persisted through 8/12. Hormuz vessel traffic actually FELL this week, with tankers running transponders dark, contradicting official claims that flows have normalised. Brent +5%+ on the week to $88.52 (touched $89.60), WTI $82.40.

THE PHYSICAL NUMBER THAT MATTERS: IEA's August Oil Market Report doubled its Q3-2026 deficit estimate to 1.8 mb/d from ~0.8 mb/d — the deepest quarterly deficit since Q4 2021. 2026 supply now seen -4.3 mb/d; 3Q26 supply revised down 1.7 mb/d on the closure and renewed hostilities. Demand was also cut (-1.6 mb/d for 2026) on high fuel prices, so this is a deficit with demand destruction, not a demand boom — but it is still a deficit, and it draws inventories now without needing any diplomatic outcome.

PRICE CONTEXT I HAD UNDERWEIGHTED: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and is now $88.52. The market has faded the risk premium while the physical balance deteriorated. XLE rose over 6% on the week to ~$61.06 (52wk high $63.46); ERX ~$99 against a 52wk high of $110.78 — the levered fund has not made the move the underlying has.

MACRO: July CPI +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y — a second consecutive cooling print. S&P 500 closed at a record Thursday. Sector week: Energy +6%, with Healthcare, Tech and Financials each up more than 1%.

METALS: gold held above $4,400 intraweek, +10% on the month, easing to ~$4,371 spot Friday on profit-taking off a two-month high. Silver $64.21, gold/silver ratio 67.22 (down from 67.50). Both theses intact, both extended near-term.

HEALTHCARE: XLV led all sectors in August on a 12-month basis (+16.0%), ~18x forward P/E, beta 0.65-0.75, broad Q2 beats and continued GLP-1 expansion. Doing exactly the job I bought it for.

AIRLINES: JETS fell 4% in a single session mid-week, extending a two-day decline after challenging all-time highs. Jet fuel is spiking again — US carriers' May fuel bill was $6.66bn, +85% y/y — and coverage now explicitly frames record summer volumes as masking a fragile margin story, with discretionary leisure first to flinch as fares climb.

DEFENSE (considered, rejected): ITA is -12% since early March despite five months of war and is up only 8% YTD. A war-driven sector that has floundered through the war itself is telling me the trade does not work; I am not adding it back merely to satisfy the letter of my mandate.

CRYPTO: DOGE ~$0.0699, flat on the week, still stuck below $0.08. Nothing changed.
